en: Thus have I heard: the Gopakamoggallāna Sutta, Discourse to Gopaka Moggallāna, from the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Venerable Ānanda was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place, not long after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna.
Now at that time King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha was having Rājagaha repaired out of fear of King Pajjota.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Ānanda dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagaha for alms.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Ānanda:
“It is still too early to wander for alms in Rājagaha.
Suppose I were to go to where the brahmin Gopakamoggallāna’s workplace is, and approach the brahmin Gopakamoggallāna there.”
Then the Venerable Ānanda went to the brahmin Gopakamoggallāna’s workplace, where the brahmin Gopakamoggallāna was.
The brahmin Gopakamoggallāna saw the Venerable Ānanda coming from afar,
and upon seeing him, he said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
“Come, venerable Ānanda.
Welcome to the venerable Ānanda.
It has been long indeed since the venerable Ānanda made this occasion for coming here.”
"Let the venerable Ānanda sit down; this seat has been prepared.
The Venerable Ānanda sat down on the prepared seat.
The brahmin Gopakamoggallāna also took a certain low seat and sat down to one side.
As he was sitting to one side, the brahmin Gopakamoggallāna said this to the Venerable Ānanda:

"Master Ānanda, is there even a single bhikkhu who possesses in every way and in all respects those qualities with which the Blessed One Gotama was endowed when he was an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha?"

“There is not, brahmin, even a single bhikkhu who is endowed in every way and in all respects with those qualities that the Blessed One was endowed with when he was an arahant, a perfectly awakened Buddha.

For that Blessed One, brahmin, was the arouser of the unarisen path, the producer of the unproduced path, the declarer of the undeclared path; he was the knower of the path, the discoverer of the path, the one skilled in the path.
But now his disciples dwell following that path, having subsequently attained it.”
Now, this conversation between the Venerable Ānanda and the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna had been left unfinished.

Then the brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, while inspecting the worksites in Rājagaha, approached the workplace of the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna, where the Venerable Ānanda was staying; having approached, he...
He exchanged greetings with the Venerable Ānanda.

When they had concluded their polite and amiable conversation, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
“For what discussion, Master Ānanda, are you gathered here now, and what was the conversation that was left unfinished?”
“Here, brahmin, the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna said this to me:

‘Is there, Master Ānanda, even a single bhikkhu who is endowed in every way, in all respects, with those qualities with which the venerable Gotama was endowed when he was an arahant, a perfectly awakened Buddha?
When this was said, brahmin, I said this to the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna:”

“There is not, brahmin, even a single bhikkhu who is endowed in every way and in all respects with those qualities with which the Blessed One was endowed when he was an arahant, a perfectly awakened Buddha.

For that Blessed One, brahmin, was the arouser of the unarisen path, the producer of the unproduced path, the declarer of the undeclared path; he was the knower of the path, the discoverer of the path, the one skilled in the path.
But his disciples now dwell following that path, having subsequently attained it.”
“This, brahmin, was our conversation that was left unfinished with the brahmin Gopakamoggallāna when you arrived. “Is there,
Master Ānanda, even a single bhikkhu who has been designated by that Master Gotama as:”
“‘This one shall be your refuge after my passing, whom you should now follow’?
“No, brahmin, there is not even a single bhikkhu who has been appointed by that Blessed One—the one who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—saying:
‘This one shall be your refuge after my passing, whom you should now follow.’”
“But, Master Ānanda, is there even a single bhikkhu who has been authorized by the Saṅgha and appointed by many elder bhikkhus, thinking:
‘After the passing away of the Blessed One, he will be our refuge,’ whom you might now set up?
“There is not, brahmin, even a single bhikkhu who has been authorized by the Saṅgha and appointed by many elder bhikkhus.”
‘After the passing away of the Blessed One, this will be our refuge,’ that we might now practice accordingly.
“But, Master Ānanda, if there is thus no refuge, what is the cause for unity?
“We are not without a refuge, brahmin.”
“We have a refuge, brahmin;
we have the Dhamma as our refuge.
“But is there, Master Ānanda, even a single bhikkhu who was designated by Master Gotama thus:”
‘After my passing away, this will be your refuge,’ which you should now practice.
Being thus questioned, you say: “No single bhikkhu, O brahmin, has been appointed by that Blessed One—the one who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—with the words:
‘After my passing away, this will be your refuge, which you should now practice.’”
“But, Master Ānanda, is there even a single bhikkhu who has been authorized by the Saṅgha and appointed by many elder bhikkhus, thinking:
‘After the passing away of our Blessed One, he will be our refuge,’ whom you might now establish?
Being thus asked, he replied: “No, brahmin, there is not even a single bhikkhu who has been authorized by the Saṅgha and appointed by many elder bhikkhus.”
‘This one will be our refuge after the Blessed One has passed away, whom we may now establish’—you said this.
Yet, when asked, ‘But Master Ānanda, if there is thus no refuge, what is the cause for unity? you replied, ‘We are not without a refuge, brahmin.’”
“‘We have a refuge, brahmin;
we have the Dhamma as our refuge,’ you say.
But how, Master Ānanda, should the meaning of this statement be understood?”

“Brahmin, there is indeed a training rule prescribed for the monks by that Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—and the Pātimokkha has been recited.
On the Uposatha day, as many of us as dwell in dependence upon a single village district all assemble together;
having assembled, we request from whichever among us it falls to recite it.”
"If, while this is being recited, there is an offense or a transgression for a bhikkhu, we shall deal with him according to the Dhamma and as instructed.
"It is not, sirs, that you are making us do it;
it is the Dhamma that makes us do it."
“Master Ānanda, is there even a single bhikkhu whom you now honor, revere, esteem, and worship; whom you honor and revere, and upon whom you rely while living?
“There is not, brahmin, even a single bhikkhu whom we now honor, revere, esteem, and worship; nor is there anyone whom we honor and revere, and upon whom we rely while living.
“But Master Ānanda, is there even a single bhikkhu who was established by that Master Gotama—”
‘This shall be your refuge after my passing, which you should now put into practice’—
when asked this, you say: ‘No single bhikkhu, brahmin, has been appointed by that Blessed One— the one who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One— saying,
“This shall be your refuge after my passing, which you should now put into practice.”’”
“But, Master Ānanda, is there even a single bhikkhu who has been authorized by the Saṅgha and appointed by many elder bhikkhus, thinking:
‘After the passing away of our Blessed One, he will be our refuge,’ whom you might now establish?
When asked thus, [Ānanda replied]: “No, brahmin, there is not even a single bhikkhu who has been authorized by the Saṅgha and appointed by many elder bhikkhus—”
‘“This one will be our refuge after the Blessed One’s passing away, whom we may now support,” so you said. When asked, ‘Is there, Master Ānanda,
even a single bhikkhu whom you now honor, respect, revere, and venerate, and whom you dwell in dependence upon,

having honored and respected him?’— being thus questioned, you replied, ‘There is not, brahmin, even a single bhikkhu whom we now honor, respect, revere, and venerate, and whom we dwell in dependence upon, having honored and respected him.’”
"But how, Master Ānanda, should the meaning of this statement be understood?
"There are, brahmin, ten qualities inspiring confidence that have been declared by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
In whomsoever these qualities are found, we now honor him, revere him, esteem him, and worship him; having honored and revered him, we dwell in dependence upon him."
Which ten?

Here, brahmin, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains in the rules of training.
He is learned, one who has retained what he has heard and accumulated what he has heard.
Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end,
which proclaim the holy life in its entirety, complete and pure— such teachings as these he has heard much of,
retained in mind, mastered through speech, examined with the mind, and well-penetrated by view.
He is content with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
He gains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, the four jhānas that constitute higher mental states and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life.
He experiences various kinds of psychic power: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one.
He becomes visible and invisible; he passes unhindered through walls, through enclosures, and through mountains, as if through space;
he dives in and out of the earth as if it were water; he walks on water without breaking the surface as if on land;
and he travels cross-legged through the sky like a winged bird.
With his hand he touches and strokes even these sun and moon, so powerful and majestic;
he exercises mastery with his body as far as the Brahma-world.
With the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, he hears both kinds of sounds—the divine and the human, whether far or near.
He understands the minds of other beings and other individuals by encompassing their minds with his own mind.
He understands a mind affected by lust as "a mind affected by lust," and he understands a mind free from lust as "a mind free from lust."
He understands a mind with hatred as ‘a mind with hatred,’ he understands a mind free from hatred as ‘a mind free from hatred,’ and he understands a mind with delusion as ‘a mind with delusion.’
He understands a mind free from delusion as ‘a mind free from delusion’;
he understands a contracted mind as ‘a contracted mind’;
he understands a distracted mind as ‘a distracted mind’.
He understands an exalted mind as ‘an exalted mind,’ he understands an unexalted mind as ‘an unexalted mind,’ and he understands a surpassable mind as ‘a surpassable mind.’
He understands an unsurpassed mind as ‘an unsurpassed mind’;
he understands a concentrated mind as ‘a concentrated mind’;
he understands an unconcentrated mind as ‘an unconcentrated mind.’
He understands a liberated mind as "a liberated mind," and he understands an unliberated mind as "an unliberated mind.
He recollects his manifold past abodes, that is to say: one birth, two births, three births... [and so on].
Whether four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births,
a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, or many aeons of world-contraction,
many aeons of world-expansion, or many aeons of both world-contraction and expansion: "In such a place I was..."
"Such was my name, such my clan, such my appearance, such my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such the limit of my lifespan;
passing away from there, I arose elsewhere. There too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, such a limit of my lifespan;
passing away from there, I reappeared here. Thus, with its aspects and particulars, he recollects his manifold past lives.
He recollects his past lives.

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma.
Through the destruction of the taints, he realizes for himself in this very life, through direct knowledge, and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.
“Brahmin, these are the ten qualities inspiring confidence that have been proclaimed by that Blessed One—the one who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Since these qualities are found in us, we now honor, revere, esteem, and worship them; having honored and revered them, we dwell in dependence upon them.
When this was said, the brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, addressed Upananda the general:
“What do you think, General, when these worthy ones honor those who should be honored, revere those who should be revered, respect those who should be respected,
and worship those who should be worshipped? “Indeed,
these worthy ones honor those who should be honored, revere those who should be revered, respect those who should be respected, and worship those who should be worshipped.”
"For if these worthy ones were not to honor, revere, esteem, and worship this [teaching],
then for what reason would those worthy ones honor, revere, esteem, and worship it, and having honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped it,
dwell in dependence upon it? Then the brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, said this to the venerable Ānanda:
“But where, venerable Ānanda, do you dwell at present?
“I dwell now, brahmin, in the Bamboo Grove.
“Is the Bamboo Grove, Master Ānanda, delightful, quiet, and free from noise; secluded from people, private from men, and suitable for retreat?”

“Indeed, brahmin, Veḷuvana is delightful, quiet, with little noise, free from the bustle of people, a place for seclusion, suitable for retreat, because it has protectors and guardians such as yourselves.

“Indeed, Master Ānanda, Veḷuvana is delightful, quiet, with little noise, free from the bustle of people, a place for seclusion, suitable for retreat, because it has meditators who are habituated to meditation such as you.
You are indeed meditators and habituated to meditation.”
"On one occasion, Master Ānanda, that venerable Gotama was staying at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.
Then, Master Ānanda, I went to the Great Wood, to the Gabled Hall, where the venerable Gotama was.
And there, the venerable Gotama spoke in many ways on the subject of meditation."
"That venerable Gotama was indeed a meditator and one whose nature was meditation;
moreover, that venerable Gotama praised all forms of meditation.
"But, brahmin, it is not the case that the Blessed One praised every kind of meditation, nor is it the case that the Blessed One did not praise every kind of meditation."
And how, brahmin, did that Blessed One not praise jhāna?
Here, brahmin, someone dwells with a mind obsessed by sensual lust, inclined toward sensual lust, and he does not understand, as it really is, the escape from arisen sensual lust.
Making sensual lust itself his internal support, he meditates, he meditates deeply, he meditates intensely, he meditates thoroughly.
He dwells with a mind obsessed by ill will, overcome by ill will, and he does not understand, as it really is, the escape from arisen ill will.
Making ill will itself his internal barrier, he meditates, he meditates deeply, he meditates intensely, he meditates thoroughly.
He dwells with a mind obsessed by sloth and torpor, overcome by sloth and torpor, and he does not understand, as it really is, the escape from arisen sloth and torpor.
Making precisely lethargy and drowsiness an obstacle, he meditates, contemplates, broods, and ponders.

He dwells with a mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse, overcome by restlessness and remorse; and not knowing, as it really is, the escape from arisen restlessness and remorse, he makes precisely restlessness and remorse an obstacle, and meditates, contemplates, broods, and ponders.
He dwells with a mind obsessed by doubt and overwhelmed by doubt; he does not understand, as it really is, the escape from arisen doubt.
Making doubt itself his internal support, he meditates, contemplates, ponders, and broods.
Such meditation, brahmin, that Blessed One did not praise.
And how, brahmin, did the Blessed One praise jhāna?

Here, brahmin, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.

With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and mental unification, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses rapture and pleasure born of concentration.
“He enters and dwells in the third jhāna… and the fourth jhāna.
It is such a jhāna as this, brahmin, that the Blessed One praised.”
“Venerable Ānanda, it seems that Master Gotama censured meditative absorption when it was blameworthy and praised it when it was praiseworthy.
Come now, venerable Ānanda, let us go;
we have many duties and much to do.”
“Now is the time for you to do as you think fit, brahmin.
Then the brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Venerable Ānanda’s words, rose from his seat and departed.
Not long after the brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, had left, the brahmin Gopakamoggallāna said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
“What we asked the venerable Ānanda, that the venerable Ānanda has not explained to us.
“Did we not tell you, brahmin:
‘Brahmin, there is not even a single bhikkhu who is endowed in every way, in all respects, with those qualities with which the Blessed One was endowed—worthy and perfectly enlightened’?”

"For it is thus, brahmin, that the Blessed One is the arouser of the unarisen path, the producer of the unproduced path, the declarer of the undeclared path; he is the knower of the path, the discoverer of the path, the one skilled in the path.
And his disciples now dwell following that path, having subsequently attained it.
The Gopakamoggallāna Sutta, the eighth, is finished.
